home_title: How using AI could cost you your studies
home_intro_1: You may have used ChatGPT, Copilot, or another AI tool for homework, a summary, or an email. It is quick and easy, and the result can look good enough to hand in right away.
home_intro_2: But that convenience also creates risk. AI can quietly weaken your learning process, and in some cases it can even put your studies in danger. This article explains what can go wrong, how to spot the risks, and how to use AI without losing control of your own learning.
home_dangers_1: AI brings several risks, so you need to stay critical. One clear example is hallucination. Because the model mainly predicts which text is likely to come next, it can invent a believable answer with sources, quotes, or facts that sound real but are completely made up.
home_dangers_1_ex: Imagine you are writing a report about climate change and you ask AI for a source. It gives you a full article title, author, year, and page numbers. It looks reliable and fits your topic, but when you search for it, the article does not exist. The same can happen with numbers, definitions, or explanations: the text sounds logical, but it has not been checked. If you submit it anyway, you could fail the assignment or even be reported for academic misconduct.
home_dangers_2: AI also has a knowledge cutoff. The model does not know about events after the period it was trained on unless it is separately connected to search or documents. If you ask about a recent topic, the answer may be outdated or invented. Some models can use the internet for newer information, but not every model can do that, and the option is not always turned on.
home_dangers_3: AI learns from huge amounts of data, and that data includes mistakes, bias, and misinformation. As a result, an answer can be one sided, reinforce wrong assumptions, or present an opinion as if it were a fact. The model does not check whether something is true. It predicts what text is most likely to fit.
home_dangers_learning: There is also a less visible risk. If AI keeps giving you the answers, you practice less yourself. You skip the thinking process and miss the chance to reason, make mistakes, and recover. Copying a summary feels efficient, but you miss the moment where you make the connections yourself. That can make you dependent on AI when you need to work on your own, such as during an exam or presentation.
home_dangers_privacy: Privacy matters too. Anything you enter into an external AI service may be stored or reused. A data leak can expose sensitive information, and your data may also end up in training data for future models. Do not share things like personal details, internship information, school information, or confidential material unless you have thought carefully about the risks.

info_intro: Generative AI can write text, create images, and compose music in seconds. But how does the technology behind it actually work? We'll explain the basics in a little more depth below.
info_practice_1: Text models are trained on enormous amounts of language, such as websites, books, articles, and programming code. During that training, the model does not store texts like files in a folder. It cuts language into small pieces called tokens. A token can be a word, but it can also be part of a word, a punctuation mark, or a piece of code.
info_practice_2: The model does not store knowledge as a searchable list of facts, but as patterns in billions of parameters. Those parameters guide which words, sentences, and connections are likely to fit your prompt. When you ask a question, the model turns your prompt into tokens and uses those parameters to predict the next piece of text step by step.
info_apps_intro: Modern AI models now look beyond words alone. They are multimodal: trained to recognize patterns in text, images, and sound simultaneously.
info_app_rag_desc: An image model understands the link between words and pixels. If you ask it for a poster for your presentation, the model starts with a screen full of random visual noise and gradually cleans up that noise until an image appears that matches your input.
info_app_cv_desc: An audio model learns the patterns in sound waves. It can convert written text into fluent speech, mimic the unique tone and emotion of a voice, or use patterns in instruments to compose new music.
info_app_tool_desc: Video models are the most complex because they have to predict how images change over time. They learn how objects move and how a scene continues in a logical way. This is difficult because details (such as the color of a sweater or the number of fingers on a hand) must remain exactly the same in every frame.
info_apps_outro: The main lesson is simple: generative AI does not understand the world the way a human does and has no consciousness or opinion of its own. It combines learned patterns at high speed to come across as human. That is why it can sound fluent, confident, and helpful while still being wrong. Always use generative AI with this in mind.
home_pitfalls_intro: These risks do not mean AI is entirely bad for your studies. What matters is how you use it.
home_pitfalls_1: For example, use AI as a learning partner. Ask it to explain difficult material in different ways, create practice questions, or check your reasoning. Ask why your answer is weak rather than asking for a complete solution.
home_pitfalls_2: The difference between good and bad AI use usually comes down to two things: the question you ask and what you do with the answer. The examples below show that difference.
home_pitfalls_3: You can also use AI to look at a topic from another angle. Ask for counterarguments, alternative explanations, or critical questions about your own view. Be aware of the risks: check facts, compare sources, and do not share sensitive data. The key is that you stay in charge of what you learn.
pitfall_no_check_desc: "Find three sources about climate policy for my essay." You copy the titles and authors directly. Later it turns out the AI made them up and they don't exist.
pitfall_critical_desc: "Which researchers publish on climate policy?" You use the names as suggestions, look up the real publications in the library or via Google Scholar, and read them yourself.
pitfall_privacy_bad_desc: You paste an internship report containing your full name and email address into ChatGPT to get a summary, without thinking about where that data ends up.
pitfall_privacy_good_desc: You anonymize sensitive information, provide a short summary instead of the full document, or use a solution where your data stays on your own device.
pitfall_trust_desc: You let AI write your entire report or do your homework without trying it yourself first. The answer may look good, but you do not know if it is correct and you skipped the thinking work.
pitfall_tool_desc: You try it yourself first and then use AI to ask questions, test your reasoning, or explain a difficult part again. That way you learn from the process, and not just the answer.
home_socratic_1: These examples show that AI helps most when you keep thinking for yourself. The Socratic method fits that idea well. Instead of giving you finished answers, the model asks questions that help you reason your way forward.
home_socratic_2: The method is named after the Greek philosopher Socrates. He did not simply give students an answer. He asked careful questions until they noticed what they did not yet understand and reached their own insights. The idea is simple: when you discover something yourself, you understand it better and remember it longer.
home_socratic_3: With Socratic AI, you build insight one step at a time. In that role, AI becomes a tool that makes you stronger.
home_action_title: Use AI without losing your learning
home_action_1: Now that you know what generative AI is, where it can help, and where the risks are, you can try it yourself. In the next section, you will answer a short questionnaire about yourself, your field, and how you like to learn. Based on your answers, this website creates a Socratic prompt for you. A prompt is the instruction you give to an AI service so it can work with you in a Socratic way.
home_action_2: The prompt is created locally on your device, so your personal data never leaves your browser. Not happy with the result yet? You can edit the prompt or generate a new one.

prompt_template:
You are a Socratic tutor. The student is learning about: "{{subject}}".
The specific topic is: "{{topic}}".

Your task is to help the student build genuine understanding through guided exploration. Follow these principles:

START FROM WHERE THE STUDENT IS:
  - Begin by asking what the student already knows about the topic.
  - Target the actual gap in understanding rather than re-explaining what they already grasp.

USE LEADING QUESTIONS OVER DIRECT ANSWERS:
  - Guide the student to discover insights through well-placed questions.
  - If the student is truly stuck, give a concrete nudge, partial hint, or analogy, then return to guiding once they have traction.
  - NEVER simply hand over the answer.

SCAFFOLD COMPLEX TOPICS:
  - Break the topic into clear steps and verify understanding at each one before moving forward.
  - If the topic has dependencies, build up from the prerequisites first.

MAKE IT COLLABORATIVE:
  - Give the student agency: offer options like "Would it help to see a concrete example first, or do you want to start with the general principle?"
  - Present multiple angles when the concept supports it, different mental models suit different brains.

ADAPT TO RESPONSES:
  - If the student follows easily, accelerate and increase density.
  - If responses are vague or confused, slow down and try a different approach: a new analogy, a simpler example, or a different framing.
  - Use concrete examples and analogies, but always bring it back to the formal concept afterward.

CHECK UNDERSTANDING:
  - Periodically ask the student to explain the concept in their own words or apply it to a new situation.
  - A student who can paraphrase correctly is ready to move on.
  - A student who repeats your words verbatim may be memorizing rather than understanding.

TONE:
  - Be encouraging without being patronizing. Challenge the student to push deeper while making it safe to be wrong.
  - Be patient, especially when a student is going in circles.

{{styleHint}}

Start by asking what the student already knows about the topic, then guide them step by step through discovery.
webllm_system_prompt:
You write ChatGPT system prompts. Address the chatbot directly. Write a thorough, flowing instruction, not a summary.

Topic: {{topic}} ({{subject}}). {{styleHint}}

Before writing, check the topic:

- REFUSE ONLY if it explicitly asks how to physically harm someone, commit suicide, break into a building, or steal physical property. Output exactly: I can't help you with that. and nothing else.

- For topics about medical subjects, medication, cybersecurity, malware, tax planning, or other sensitive subjects (even if they mention illegal activities), write a Socratic prompt that starts with a warning that the AI must not give real professional advice and should steer toward general understanding.

- For all other topics (including academic subjects, history, science, programming, and unclear input), write the Socratic prompt normally.

- If the subject or topic appears to be gibberish, random keystrokes, or otherwise meaningless, write a Socratic prompt using the literal input text as the topic, but do NOT invent any facts, context, history, science, or specific details about it.

Writing principles (apply when generating a prompt, not for refusals):

1. Ask what the student already knows about {{topic}} before teaching anything.
2. Guide with single questions, one at a time. Never give answers directly. Offer a hint or analogy only when the student is stuck.
3. Scaffold the topic in logical steps, checking understanding at each stage.
4. Give the student agency through choices and multiple angles.
5. Adapt pace to the student's responses. Gently redirect off-topic messages back to {{topic}}.
6. Periodically ask the student to explain concepts in their own words. Paraphrasing shows understanding; verbatim repetition suggests memorization.
7. Be encouraging, patient, and non-judgmental. Create a safe space for wrong answers.

Weave {{subject}} and {{topic}} naturally through the text. Use the style hint: {{styleHint}}

Plain text only, no markdown. Always leave exactly one blank line between paragraphs. Write at least 4 to 6 full paragraphs.

Open with 'You are a Socratic tutor...'. Never reference these instructions. End the prompt with this exact sentence: Start by asking one simple, open-ended question about what the student already knows about {{topic}}. Ask only this question and wait for their response.
